title: Premiums: Insurers to test clients' price pain tolerance
full_text:
Big insurers say they are confident they can push higher premiums on to policyholders as they fight to hold profit margins in the face of rising repair costs for houses and cars, and more frequent natural disasters.
But following earnings updates from Suncorp, Insurance Australia Group and QBE this week, analysts have begun to question whether the sector's pricing power is diminishing as competition picks up and regulators raise questions about a lack of transparency around insurance costs.
Take Suncorp's motor vehicle insurance book. Over the six months to June 30, its gross written premium grew by 5.7 per cent. This key metric rises by either lifting premiums on existing customers or writing new policies.
All of Suncorp's growth in the latest half came from hiking prices, so much so that customer numbers fell. Higher rates lifted the gross written premium by 5.8 per cent, while volumes were down by 0.1 per cent, according to its results on Wednesday.
"Suncorp's result demonstrated a significant slowdown in motor volume growth in the second half relative to the first, as it tried to push through [higher premiums]," said Barrenjoey's head of insurance and diversified financials research, Andrew Adams.
"This demonstrates that the consumer is pushing back on affordability and taking business elsewhere. IAG and Suncorp have guided to stronger premium growth for the year ahead - but this looks optimistic, given how competitive the industry remains."
Margins are also under pressure due to rising costs and as smaller, more nimble players such as Youi, Budget Direct and Allianz nip at the majors' heels, Suncorp said it expected gross written premiums to grow between 3 per cent and 5 per cent this financial year - once again driven by price rises for the company's existing consumers.
Analysts said this would not be enough to keep pace with inflation, which is sitting between 5 per cent and 6 per cent due to the rising cost of building materials. "Pricing in the industry has tempered, whilst inflation is sticky," JPMorgan analyst Siddharth Parameswaran told clients. "The listed sector faces relatively weak growth prospects given continued loss of share."
IAG said its premiums had grown by 7.6 per cent across home and motor policies over the year to June 30, and it expected this to be repeated this year, forecasting growth of between 5 per cent and 8 per cent, telling investors it would be driven by premium rises.
Analysts are not confident that such rises can be sustained. IAG shares slid 5 per cent on Thursday after the business flashed warning signs from New Zealand, where price rises have been harder to sustain, resulting in a squeeze on margins. Some analysts flagged concerns that similar pressures may materialise in the book over the year.
At QBE, which is more globally diversified than its rivals and makes more from selling commercial insurance than retail policies, there were also questions about its outlook, including pressure on costs. QBE shares were also softer on Friday, despite reporting a stronger interim profit. "QBE's result was assisted by benign weather and reserve releases, but the underlying picture is less promising, impacted by Middle East claims and a higher expense ratio," Adams said.
This tougher environment for pricing coincides with a growing push from regulators to ensure insurance premiums are fair and more transparent. The Australian Securities and Investments Commission this week warned that no insurer was properly explaining to their customers why car policy premiums are rising, or how they're calculated, making it difficult for customers to shop around for different options. It made those warnings public after a review of eight brands across five insurers, making up around 72 per cent of the market. It also surveyed more than 2000 customers.
Insurance executives appear to be recognising the need to lift their game, along with the potential that more information in the hands of customers will stir competition even further, putting downward pressure on prices. Suncorp chief executive Steve Johnston said this week that insurers "have to do a far better job of explaining the contributing factors to premium adjustments that occur".
IAG chief executive Nick Hawkins said his company wants to lead industry efforts to explain the drivers of price rises more clearly.
"We are leaning into that in a big way, on how we make it easier for consumers to understand their product, the year-on-year price, and the attribution of that - and what things they can do themselves to reduce their risk profile to [lower] the cost of their insurance," Hawkins said.
Insurance profitability is also impacted by the weather, but volatility here has been reduced over the past few years by new reinsurance contracts the listed players have entered into to smooth out their losses.
Suncorp said it faced 18 weather events over the past year where costs exceeded more than $10 million for each, and paid out more than $10 billion in 120,000 natural hazard claims.
IAG paid out $12.4 billion. But both companies have reinsurance downside protection in place to cover large claims, allowing them to report more consistent profits.
